turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell expressed her incredulity, asking Jack how he could possibly expect to be considered a suitable husband for her daughter when he was so careless with the truth.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained that he must have made a mistake, that he had been thinking of his other house in Belgrave Square when he gave the number.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack that she was shocked that he would so readily admit to making a mistake, and that she feared it was a sign of a deeper lack of responsibility.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen told the carriage driver to let her down and that she would rather hear the rest of the conversation from the hallway than remain confined to the carriage.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell insisted that Jack provide a satisfactory explanation for his error, and that he must be prepared to answer further questions about his background and character.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained that he was not trying to deceive, but rather was simply unsure of the exact number of his houses, and that he had only recently acquired the one in Upper Norfold Gardens.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell asked Jack for a detailed account of his financial situation, expressing a keen interest in knowing how he planned to support his future wife, Gwendolen, in the manner to which she was accustomed.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen declared that she would not be treated like some sort of chattel, that she had a say in her own life and marriage, and that she would not be lectured to by her mother as if she were a child.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell turned to Gwendolen with a stern expression and told her that she would not be lectured by her mother, and that her concerns about her daughter's marriage were entirely justified.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained that he had always assumed that his family's financial situation would be sufficient to support his future wife, and he had not thought to disclose any further details.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell expressed her deep disappointment in Jack's lack of transparency regarding his financial situation, stating that a suitable husband for her daughter must be able to provide for her in a manner befitting her station.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained that he had been under the impression that his family's reputation and connections were more important than their actual financial situation, and that he had hoped Lady Bracknell would understand the value of marrying into a respectable family.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack that his family's reputation and connections, while respectable, were not sufficient to offset the fact that his father's fortune was being squandered on his brother's reckless business ventures.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained that his brother's business ventures were, in fact, quite successful, and that his father's investment in them would likely yield a substantial profit in the near future.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell's expression turned stern as she told Jack that she would not be swayed by empty promises of future financial success, and that only tangible evidence of his family's solvency would suffice.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack humbly asked Lady Bracknell if he might be given the opportunity to retrieve the documents proving his family's financial stability, explaining that they were currently in his father's study.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen told Jack that she was fed up with this inquisition and that she had every intention of marrying him, regardless of his family's financial situation.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack asked Lady Bracknell if she might consider his fiancée's feelings, and whether it would be possible to proceed with the discussion of his family's finances in a less...formal atmosphere.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell told Gwendolen that she would not be influenced by her daughter's whims and that the discussion of Jack's suitability as a husband would continue as before, regardless of Gwendolen's feelings.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen exclaimed that her mother's behavior was outrageous and that she would not stand for it, and that she insisted that they be allowed to leave immediately if the interrogation continued.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen told Lady Bracknell that she was engaged to Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Gwendolen and Mr. Worthing to pardon her, as they were not engaged to anyone. She explained that when they did become engaged, she or Mr. Worthing's father, if his health permitted, would inform them of the fact. An engagement should come as a surprise to a young girl, and it was hardly a matter she could arrange for herself. While she was making inquiries, Gwendolen would wait for her below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen called out to Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Gwendolen to wait for her in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen replied to Lady Bracknell that she would wait for her.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Mr. Worthing to take a seat.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack stood tall, his eyes locked on Lady Bracknell, and said that he preferred to remain standing, rather than take a seat.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell informed Mr. Worthing that he was not on her list of eligible young men, although she had the same list as the Duchess of Bolton. However, she was willing to enter his name if his answers were satisfactory. She asked him if he smoked.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing admitted to Lady Bracknell that he smoked.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell was pleased to hear that Mr. Worthing smoked. She believed that a man should have an occupation. There were too many idle men in London. She asked Mr. Worthing how old he was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he was twenty-nine.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell thought that twenty-nine was a good age to get married. She believed that a man who wanted to get married should know either everything or nothing. She asked Mr. Worthing which category he fell into.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing replied to Lady Bracknell that he knew nothing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell was pleased to hear that Mr. Worthing knew nothing. She believed that ignorance was a delicate and exotic fruit that should not be tampered with. She stated that education was unsound and produced no effect in England. If it did, it would be a danger to the upper classes. She asked Mr. Worthing about his income.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that his income was between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing if his income came from land or investments.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing replied to Lady Bracknell that his income came from investments.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell thought that Mr. Worthing's income was satisfactory. She stated that land was no longer a profit or pleasure, but rather a means of gaining position and losing it. She asked Mr. Worthing about his country house.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he had a country house with some land, but he did not depend on it for his income. In fact, the poachers were the only ones who made anything out of it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing how many bedrooms his country house had. She also asked if he had a town house, as a girl like Gwendolen could not be expected to reside in the country.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he owned a house in Belgrave Square, but it was let by the year to Lady Bloxham.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing who Lady Bloxham was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack observed that Lady Bracknell went out very little, and that she was a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing what number his house in Belgrave Square was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that his house was number 149.
